Annuity income and liquid capital: read the cash flows before interpreting the payout

Four graphics explain an illustrative premium allocation, conditional lifetime receipts, inflation and why a payout percentage is not an investment return.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

The central idea

An income contract can replace part of a liquid portfolio with scheduled payments. Compare the payment, liquidity, inflation exposure and contract terms without treating cumulative receipts as an annual yield.

01

Distinguish income from an accessible account balance

The FCAC’s annuity guide distinguishes life income from fixed-term payments and describes options for survivors or beneficiaries. It also explains that payments can combine interest, returned capital and risk pooling. A payout amount therefore cannot be read as investment interest alone.

This illustration assumes an immediate level-payment life-only contract. Every displayed receipt is conditional on the annuitant remaining alive. No guarantee period, survivor continuation, death benefit, tax calculation or contract surrender value is included.

The entered payment per CAD 100,000 of premium is hypothetical, not an available insurer quote. The model scales it linearly with the selected premium allocation. Actual products, pricing and terms require separate verification. The graph does not estimate an expected lifetime payout or assign a probability to the selected payment horizon.

02

See what remains liquid after the allocation

The default illustration begins with CAD 500,000 of liquid capital and allocates 40%, or CAD 200,000, to the income contract. The waterfall leaves CAD 300,000 of liquid capital at the purchase date.

The premium has been exchanged for contractual income. It is not labelled an immediate investment loss or a fee. Equally, it is not still available as cash for a separate purchase. The tool does not value the contract, so the waterfall endpoint is liquid capital rather than total wealth.

The remaining liquid amount has no modeled return or withdrawal schedule here. A complete retirement budget would assign that money to reserves, future spending or other purposes, and compare those uses with the income supplied by the contract.

03

A payout percentage does not isolate investment return

The default hypothetical payment is CAD 550 a month for each CAD 100,000 of premium. On CAD 200,000, that produces CAD 1,100 a month, or CAD 13,200 over twelve payments. Annual cash paid divided by premium is 6.6%.

That 6.6% is a cash-payout ratio. It does not separate interest from returned capital or pooling, and it assumes neither a redeemable principal balance nor a residual estate value. It is not directly comparable with a savings-account interest rate or a portfolio’s total return.

The cumulative-receipts chart compares the original premium with payments actually assumed to occur. At CAD 1,100 per month, 181 receipts total CAD 199,100 and 182 total CAD 200,200. The nominal cash-receipt crossover is therefore 182 months, or fifteen years and two months, conditional on receiving every payment.

04

Keep the receipt crossover separate from inflation and opportunity cost

After thirty years of the selected payments, cumulative gross receipts total CAD 396,000. Comparing that sum with the CAD 200,000 premium does not account for when each receipt arrived, tax, inflation or returns that an alternative arrangement might have produced.

The purchasing-power chart isolates one of those issues. The nominal monthly amount remains CAD 1,100. With 2% annual inflation, its purchasing power after thirty years is approximately CAD 607.28 in purchase-date dollars. The year-zero point is a comparison of payment amounts, not a payment received at purchase.

An indexed payment would require its own terms and quote. This tool does not assume that an increasing payment can be purchased for the same premium and initial amount. The constant-payment illustration simply makes the price exposure visible.

05

Compare contracts and household needs on the same basis

The matrix shows cumulative gross payments as a percentage of a fixed CAD 100,000 premium at several hypothetical monthly amounts and durations. A cell above 100% means nominal cash received exceeds that premium, conditional on all the displayed payments occurring.

It is not a gain after opportunity cost, an annual rate, an insurer offer or a survival probability. The fixed grid remains independent of the selected allocation. Choosing zero allocation leaves the selected payment at zero and reports no premium-receipt crossover.

The FCAC guide also notes that contract options, tax treatment and the ability to change or cancel vary. Review those terms alongside other household income, the need for accessible cash and the treatment of a survivor or estate. The four graphics support that cash-flow discussion without deciding whether an annuity is suitable or ranking it against an investment portfolio.
